cards.title: 3.1 Fundamental Wave Mechanics and Wave Behaviors
body: 3.1 Fundamental Wave Mechanics and Wave Behaviors
A **wave** is a repeating disturbance or oscillation that travels through space-time, accompanied by a transfer of energy from one point to another without the permanent physical transport of matter.

Waves are categorized into two fundamental classes based on their propagation mechanisms: mechanical and electromagnetic. **Mechanical waves** require a physical medium (such as a solid, liquid, or gas) to travel. Examples include water ripples, slinky waves, and sound. These waves propagate because adjacent particles within the medium collide, transferring kinetic energy from one particle to the next. In contrast, **electromagnetic waves** (including visible light, radio waves, and X-rays) do not require a material medium. They consist of mutually perpendicular electric and magnetic field oscillations and propagate through empty space

cards.title: Waves and Sound
body:
When a wave encounters a boundary between different media, several fundamental behaviors occur:
1. **Reflection**: The wave bounces off the boundary and returns to its original medium. If a wave on a string hits a fixed boundary, the reflected pulse is inverted (upside down); if the boundary is free, the reflected pulse is not inverted.
2. **Refraction**: The wave crosses into the second medium, changing its speed and wavelength, which causes its direction of propagation to bend. Refraction is governed by the law of refraction:
$$\frac{\sin i}{\sin r} = \frac{v_1}{v_2}$$

cards.title: Waves and Sound
body: > **💡 Did You Know?**: Earthquakes produce both longitudinal and transverse mechanical waves. Seismologists discovered that only longitudinal waves (P-waves) can travel through the Earth's liquid outer core, while transverse waves (S-waves) are blocked. This provided the first definitive proof that the Earth's outer core is liquid.

> **🧠 Pro-Tip**: When a wave transitions from one medium to another, its speed and wavelength change, but its **frequency remains constant** because it is determined solely by the source of the oscillation.

cards.title: 3.2 Sound Waves: Production, Speed, and Behavior
body: 3.2 Sound Waves: Production, Speed, and Behavior

**Sound** is a mechanical, longitudinal wave produced by vibrating objects, propagating through a compressible medium (solid, liquid, or gas) via a series of alternating high-pressure regions (compressions) and low-pressure regions (rarefactions).

All sounds originate from vibrating matter. For instance, when you speak, your vocal cords vibrate, forcing surrounding air molecules to oscillate. Because sound is a mechanical wave, it requires a material medium to travel. It cannot propagate through a vacuum because there are no particles to transmit collisions. This is demonstrated by the classic bell jar experiment: as air is pumped out of a jar containing a ringing electric bell, the sound becomes progressively fainter until it dies away completely, even though the hammer can still be seen striking the bell.

cards.title: Study Notes worked
cards.problem: At constant wave speed, what is the mathematical relationship between wavelength ($$\lambda$$) and frequency ($$f$$)?

steps.text: **Step 2: Analyze the proportionality at constant speed**
If $$v$$ is constant, then $$\lambda$$ is inversely proportional to $$f$$. This means that as frequency increases, wavelength decreases proportionally.
Therefore, **Wavelength is inversely proportional to frequency**.

cards.title: Study Notes worked
cards.problem: Sound waves cannot travel through which of the following?

steps.text: Sound is a mechanical wave. Mechanical waves require a physical medium composed of particles to transmit oscillations via collisions.
A vacuum contains no particles. Therefore, there are no particles to collide and transmit energy, meaning sound cannot travel through it.
Therefore, sound cannot travel through **a vacuum**.

Additionally, waves are classified by the direction of particle oscillation relative to the direction of wave propagation. In a **transverse wave**, the particles of the medium oscillate perpendicular (at right angles) to the direction of energy transport. Light, waves on a vibrating string, and surface water waves are prime examples. In a **longitudinal wave**, the particles of the medium oscillate parallel to the direction of energy transport, creating alternating regions of high density (**compressions**) and low density (**rarefactions**). Sound waves are the most common longitudinal waves.

4. **Interference**: When two or more waves travel through the same medium simultaneously, they overlap. According to the *Principle of Superposition*, the resulting displacement is the algebraic sum of the individual wave displacements. If the waves are in phase, they reinforce each other (**constructive interference**), producing a larger amplitude. If they are out of phase, they cancel each other out (**destructive interference**).

cards.title: Study Notes worked
cards.problem: A transverse wave is transporting energy from east to west. In which direction do the particles of the medium oscillate?

steps.text: **Step 1: Recall the definition of a transverse wave**
In a transverse wave, the particles of the medium oscillate perpendicular (at right angles) to the direction of wave propagation.
If the energy transport (wave direction) is horizontal (east to west), the perpendicular oscillation must be vertical (upward and downward).
Therefore, particles move **both upward and downward, perpendicular to east-west**.

cards.title: Study Notes worked
cards.problem: Which of the following physical properties primarily determines the speed of a mechanical wave?

steps.text: - While the wave equation $$v = f \lambda$$ relates speed to frequency and wavelength, the physical speed $$v$$ of a mechanical wave is determined solely by the properties of the medium through which it travels, specifically its elasticity and density.
- Amplitude, frequency, and wavelength do not change the speed of a wave in a uniform medium.
Therefore, the speed is determined by **the physical properties of the medium**.

cards.title: Study Notes worked
cards.problem: Through which of the following media does a sound wave travel the fastest?

steps.text: Sound travels fastest in solids, slower in liquids, and slowest in gases. This is because solids have high elastic properties (bulk modulus) and closely packed atoms, allowing rapid momentum transfer.

cards.title: Waves and Sound
body: To analyze wave motion mathematically, we define several critical parameters. The *amplitude* ($$A$$) is the maximum displacement of a particle from its equilibrium position. The *wavelength* ($$\lambda$$) is the distance between any two adjacent in-phase points, such as successive crests in a transverse wave or successive compressions in a longitudinal wave. The *frequency* ($$f$$) is the number of complete wave cycles that pass a given point in one second, measured in Hertz ($$\text{Hz}$$, where $$1 \text{ Hz} = 1 \text{ s}^{-1}$$$). The *period* ($$T$$) is the time required for one complete wave cycle to pass a fixed point, which is the reciprocal of frequency:
These variables are related to the wave speed ($$v$$) by the fundamental **wave equation**:
$$v = f \lambda = \frac{\lambda}{T}$$

cards.title: Waves and Sound
body:
| Parameter | Definition | SI Unit | Formula / Relationship |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Amplitude ($$A$$)** | Maximum displacement from equilibrium | Meter ($$\text{m}$$) | Determined by wave energy |
| **Wavelength ($$\lambda$$)** | Distance between successive identical points | Meter ($$\text{m}$$) | $$\lambda = \frac{v}{f}$$ |
| **Frequency ($$f$$)** | Number of cycles passing a point per second | Hertz ($$\text{Hz}$$) | $$f = \frac{1}{T}$$ |
| **Period ($$T$$)** | Time taken for one complete cycle | Second ($$\text{s}$$) | $$T = \frac{1}{f}$$ |
| **Speed ($$v$$)** | Distance traveled by a wave per unit time | Meter per second ($$\text{m/s}$$) | $$v = f \lambda$$ |

cards.problem: In a longitudinal wave, the regions where the particles of the medium are spread furthest apart are called:

steps.text: Longitudinal waves consist of alternating compressions and rarefactions.
- Compressions are regions where particles are crowded close together (high density).
- Rarefactions are regions where particles are spread furthest apart (low density).
